pharm: Long-acting, non-competitive (irreversible) alpha-adrenergic antagonist that covalently blocks alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, producing prolonged vasodilation and 'chemical sympathectomy'; used chiefly to control catecholamine effects in pheochromocytoma.
quick: Start 10 mg by mouth twice daily; increase every other day (usual 20-40 mg 2-3 times daily) to control blood pressure/symptoms
May give with food to reduce GI upset
Use only if clearly needed (used for pheochromocytoma in pregnancy under specialist care); neonatal hypotension/CNS effects possible
Caution - hypotension may reduce renal perfusion; no defined adjustment
Blood pressure (orthostatic), heart rate (reflex tachycardia), volume status, symptom control
summary: Phenoxybenzamine is a long-acting, non-selective, IRREVERSIBLE alpha-adrenergic receptor blocker (haloalkylamine) used chiefly to control hypertension and sweating associated with pheochromocytoma, and to treat episodes/sequelae of pheochromocytoma. By forming a covalent, non-competitive bond with alpha-1 (and alpha-2) adrenergic receptors, it produces a prolonged 'chemical sympathectomy' that cannot be overcome by increasing catecholamine levels; effects last until new receptors are synthesized (days). This lowers peripheral vascular resistance and blood pressure and prevents catecholamine-driven vasoconstriction, but characteristically causes orthostatic hypotension and a compensatory REFLEX TACHYCARDIA (so a beta-blocker may be added only AFTER adequate alpha blockade to avoid unopposed alpha effects). It is also used (often off-label) for micturition difficulty due to neurogenic bladder/partial obstruction. It is contraindicated where a fall in blood pressure is dangerous. Onset of action is slow, and effects accumulate over several days because of the irreversible mechanism. Long-term high-dose use has been associated with tumorigenicity in animals.
indications: Pheochromocytoma - to control episodes of hypertension and sweating (preoperative preparation and chronic management)
Treatment of conditions associated with excessive catecholamine effects from pheochromocytoma
Symptomatic relief of micturition difficulty (urinary outflow/neurogenic bladder) - per some labeling/regional use (off-label in many regions)

dosage.d: Initial 10 mg twice daily; increase by 10 mg every other day until blood pressure controlled and symptoms relieved; usual maintenance 20-40 mg 2-3 times daily
dosage.n: Titrate slowly; ensure adequate volume; add beta-blocker only after full alpha blockade

dosage.d: Initial ~0.2 mg/kg (max 10 mg) once daily, titrated by 0.2 mg/kg increments; usual 0.4-1.2 mg/kg/day in divided doses
Lower titrated doses per response (e.g., 10 mg daily increasing as needed)
dosage.n: Off-label in many regions; titrate to symptom relief and blood pressure tolerance

admin: Administer orally; may take with food to reduce gastrointestinal irritation
Titrate the dose slowly (increase every other day) to the lowest dose that controls blood pressure and symptoms while limiting orthostatic hypotension
Ensure adequate intravascular volume (alpha blockade unmasks/contributes to relative hypovolemia)
If a beta-blocker is needed (e.g., for reflex tachycardia or catecholamine-secreting tumor), start it only AFTER adequate alpha blockade to avoid an unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis
Allow several days for full effect because the receptor block is irreversible and cumulative
moa: Phenoxybenzamine is a haloalkylamine that produces non-competitive, irreversible alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade. It cyclizes to a highly reactive carbonium/ethyleniminium intermediate that covalently alkylates alpha-1 (and to a lesser degree alpha-2) adrenergic receptors, forming a stable, essentially permanent bond. Because the blockade is non-competitive, it cannot be overcome by raising catecholamine concentrations, and its effect persists until the receptors are regenerated (over days). The result is blockade of catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction, reduced peripheral vascular resistance, increased peripheral blood flow, and lowered blood pressure - a 'chemical sympathectomy.' Loss of alpha-mediated counter-regulation, together with any beta-mediated effects, commonly produces reflex tachycardia and postural hypotension. Phenoxybenzamine also has some antagonist activity at histamine, acetylcholine, and serotonin receptors.

absolute: Conditions in which a fall in blood pressure would be undesirable or dangerous
Known hypersensitivity to phenoxybenzamine or any component
relative: Marked cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease (hypotension may compromise perfusion)
Renal impairment (hypotension may worsen renal function)
Conditions where reflex tachycardia is hazardous
monitor: Volume status and signs of compromised organ perfusion

preg: There are limited data. Phenoxybenzamine has been used to manage pheochromocytoma in pregnancy under specialist supervision because untreated catecholamine excess is dangerous to mother and fetus. It crosses the placenta; perinatal hypotension and central nervous system depression have been reported in newborns. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk, and monitor the neonate.
lact: It is not known whether phenoxybenzamine is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse effects (e.g., hypotension) in a nursing infant, caution is advised; weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against potential risk.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established. Use with caution because phenoxybenzamine-induced hypotension can reduce renal blood flow and worsen renal function; monitor blood pressure and renal status.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; the drug is metabolized, and impaired clearance could prolong or intensify effects. Titrate carefully and monitor.

major: Sympathomimetics with mixed alpha/beta activity (e.g., epinephrine) - alpha effects are blocked, leaving unopposed beta-mediated vasodilation and worsening hypotension/tachycardia ('epinephrine reversal') - avoid epinephrine to treat phenoxybenzamine overdose
Other antihypertensives and vasodilators - additive, possibly severe, hypotension
moderate: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and nitrates - additive hypotension
Beta-blockers - useful for reflex tachycardia but must follow adequate alpha blockade to avoid unopposed alpha effects
Drugs causing orthostasis (diuretics, alcohol) - additive postural hypotension
minor: Decongestants/OTC sympathomimetics - blunted or altered pressor response
interactions.food: May be taken with food to reduce gastrointestinal irritation; no major food interaction.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - alcohol augments vasodilation and hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: May interfere with assessment of catecholamine-mediated responses; no major specific lab interference noted in labeling.

serious: Severe hypotension / shock-like state, especially after first doses or with volume depletion
Cerebral or myocardial ischemia from hypotension in patients with vascular disease
emergency: Severe symptomatic hypotension / syncope and shock
Myocardial ischemia or stroke precipitated by hypotension

monitoring: Blood pressure (supine and standing) and heart rate during titration and maintenance
Symptoms of orthostatic hypotension (dizziness, syncope) and reflex tachycardia
Volume status; ensure adequate hydration, especially perioperatively for pheochromocytoma
Adequacy of alpha blockade before adding any beta-blocker
counsel: This medicine relaxes blood vessels to control blood pressure and symptoms from a catecholamine-producing tumor; it works for several days because the effect builds up
Stand up slowly from sitting or lying down - dizziness or fainting from a drop in blood pressure is common, especially when you start or after a dose increase
You may notice a faster heartbeat, a stuffy nose, smaller pupils, or problems with ejaculation; tell your doctor if these are troublesome
Avoid alcohol and hot environments, and stay well hydrated to limit dizziness
Do not stop or change the dose on your own, and tell other doctors you take this before surgery or before receiving adrenaline-type drugs
pk: Slow onset over several hours; full effect develops over days because the block is irreversible
Effects accumulate with repeated dosing; oral absorption is incomplete/variable (~20-30%)
Plasma half-life approximately 24 hours, but pharmacologic effect outlasts plasma levels (irreversible binding)
Prolonged - effects persist 3-4 days or longer until new alpha receptors are synthesized
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light and moisture; keep out of reach of children
pearls: IRREVERSIBLE (non-competitive) alpha-1 and alpha-2 blocker - the effect cannot be overcome by catecholamines and persists for days ('chemical sympathectomy')
Mainstay of preoperative blood-pressure control in PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA; ensure adequate volume expansion during preparation
Causes orthostatic hypotension and characteristic REFLEX TACHYCARDIA - add a beta-blocker only AFTER adequate alpha blockade to avoid an unopposed-alpha hypertensive crisis
Do NOT use epinephrine to treat overdose-induced hypotension - alpha blockade leaves unopposed beta vasodilation ('epinephrine reversal'); use norepinephrine and fluids instead
Slow onset and cumulative effect mean dose titration every other day; counsel on postural symptoms and nasal stuffiness/miosis
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue the regular schedule - do not double up, as this increases the risk of severe hypotension and dizziness.
overdose: Overdose causes exaggerated pharmacologic effects: postural hypotension with dizziness or fainting, reflex tachycardia, shock, vomiting, lethargy, and sedation. Treatment is supportive: lay the patient flat with legs elevated (Trendelenburg) and give intravenous fluids to expand volume. Because alpha receptors are blocked, do NOT use epinephrine (its alpha effects are blocked, leaving unopposed beta-vasodilation that worsens hypotension - 'epinephrine reversal'); if a vasopressor is required, norepinephrine (levarterenol) may be used. Effects are prolonged owing to the irreversible blockade, so continued monitoring and supportive care are needed.
